tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__resize_window
tools.description: Emulate a viewport size in the Browser pane tab. Presets: mobile (375x812), tablet (768x1024), or desktop, which clears the size emulation and returns the tab to the pane's own responsive size. Custom sizes need both width and height. An emulated size applies to that tab across reloads and navigation (scaled down to fit when it is larger than the pane): reset it with preset "desktop" as soon as you finish testing. The desktop app may also clear a size you set when your turn ends, so set it again in a later turn if you still need it. A size the user picked from the pane's own Viewport menu is theirs and stays until they or you change it; leave it unless they ask. colorScheme (light/dark) emulates prefers-color-scheme on that tab; it survives reloads and preset "desktop" does not touch it, but the pane re-syncs the tab to the app's light/dark theme when that theme changes or the pane reopens; local documents and static HTML previews always render light. The mobile preset (and any width < 768) also emulates a mobile device: Android Chrome user agent and 5 touch points, so pages detect a touch phone; your clicks still arrive as mouse clicks. Reload the page after switching so load-time device gates re-run.

loading_messages.description: 1–4 loading messages shown to the user while the visual renders, each roughly 5 words long. Write them in the same language the user is using. Use 1 for simple visuals, more for complex ones. If the topic is serious — illness, disease, pandemics, death, grief, war, conflict, poverty, disaster, trauma, abuse, addiction, medical decisions, politically charged subjects, or anything where the reader might be personally affected — keep these BORING: describe what the code is doing in the dullest generic way, no jargon-as-drama, no evocative terms. Pandemic growth model — NOT ['Simulating patient zero', 'Modeling the curve'] (documentary-narrator voice), YES ['Setting up the model', 'Running the calculation']. Cancer timeline — NOT ['Charting the battle ahead'], YES ['Laying out the stages']. If you have to ask whether it's serious, it is. Otherwise, have fun — reach for alliteration, puns, personification, wordplay, whatever lands in that language. Playful examples — revenue chart: ['Bribing bars to stand taller', 'Asking Q4 where it went']; kanban: ['Herding cards into columns', 'Dragging, dropping, not stopping'].

572	### 4.3 Entire as episodic memory
573	
574	#### 4.3.1 Setup and capture [V]
575	
576	- `entire enable` MUST be run in every repository **before its first commit**: each host, `kintsugi-omega`, `kintsugi-antibodies` and `sabotage-log`. It installs the agent and git hooks.
577	- Checkpoints are created when the agent or a human makes a git commit (manual-commit strategy), or after each agent response (auto-commit strategy).
578	- Entire **never commits to the active branch**. Session metadata lives on the `entire/checkpoints/v1` branch.
579	- Each checkpoint captures:
580	  - the full transcript (prompts and responses);
581	  - file changes;
582	  - tool calls (commands run, files read);
583	  - token usage and timestamps;
584	  - sub-agents spawned through Claude Code's Task tool, as nested sessions.
585	- **Strategy choice.** Surgeons use the manual-commit strategy, so **one checkpoint corresponds to exactly one hypothesis attempt**. The proof bundle can then list every attempt, including failed ones.
586	
587	#### 4.3.2 Recovering intent (why the code exists)
588	
589	```
590	1. Localize      entire graph search / explain / impact     → file:line ranges + symbols
591	2. Blame         git blame -L <range> --porcelain           → commit SHAs
592	3. Map           commit → Entire checkpoint                  [A: read checkpoint metadata on
593	                                                              entire/checkpoints/v1; fallback:
594	                                                              `entire explain` on the commit [V]]
595	4. Explain       entire explain <checkpoint|commit>          → session transcript summary
596	5. Extract       Archivist (Opus) → Intent Record (below); every clause MUST cite a verbatim quote
597	6. Verify        Auditor checks each quote appears verbatim in the checkpoint transcript (G5 precondition)
598	```
599	
600	```yaml
601	intent_record:
602	  checkpoint: "ck_7f3a…"              # Entire checkpoint id
603	  commit: "c0ffee1…"
604	  session: "claude-code:…"            # agent session that authored the change
605	  stated_goal: "Refactor retry logic for readability"
606	  behavioral_contract:
607	    - clause: "No behavior change intended"
608	      quote: "…keep behavior identical, this is purely a readability refactor…"   # verbatim, ≤300 chars
609	  confidence: 0.86
610	```
611	
612	Requiring quotes is the anti-hallucination rule. A contract clause without a verbatim quote is dropped.
613	
614	#### 4.3.3 Bisecting across checkpoints
615	
616	When the replay cassette passes at an older commit, the incident is a **regression**, and the Archivist runs:
617	
618	```bash
619	git bisect start <bad_sha> <good_sha>
620	git bisect run kintsugi replay --cassette cas/INC-0042.yaml --seeds 3   # exit 0 = good, 1 = bad
621	```
622	
623	Each bisect step is annotated with its Entire checkpoint. The output is the **first bad checkpoint**: the exact AI session, and therefore the exact prompt, that introduced the regression.
624	
625	#### 4.3.4 Rewind and resume
626	
627	- Rewind:
628	  - `entire checkpoint rewind --list` lists rewind points as JSON;
629	  - `entire checkpoint rewind --to <id>` restores to one of them;
630	  - older builds use `entire rewind`;
631	  - `--logs-only` restores logs without touching the working tree.
632	- `--reset` is destructive and MUST NOT be used in autonomous mode.
633	- `entire resume <branch>` checks out the branch and restores the latest checkpointed session metadata [V]. It is used on the L2 recovery path for in-place sessions.
634	- **Honest scope.** Surgeons work in disposable worktrees, so rewinding a failed hypothesis means *discard the worktree and keep its checkpoint as evidence*. In-place rewinds are used by long-lived sessions: the Immunologist's refinement sessions and L2 orphan recovery.
635	
636	### 4.4 Entire's entire-graph as the body map [V]
637	
638	entire-graph is an Entire CLI plugin (`entire graph …`). It parses the repository locally with tree-sitter, never sends code to a model or service, maps files, symbols and relations (callers, callees, type usage), and uses limited git history to find files that change together.
639	
640	#### 4.4.1 Per-repository setup
641	
642	| Command | Purpose in Omega |
643	|---|---|
644	| `entire graph init-agents --repo .` | Writes `.entire/graph-agent.md` and managed blocks in `AGENTS.md` and `CLAUDE.md`, so every Surgeon's Claude Code session uses the graph automatically |
645	| `entire graph index` | Builds the committed-tree cache before batches of `--head` queries |
646	| `entire graph capabilities --json` | Lists supported semantic languages and **relation types**. The motif language MUST only use relations listed here. |
647	| `entire graph doctor --json` | Health check, run in the Watchdog's checks |
648	
649	#### 4.4.2 Localisation, impact and change analysis
650	
651	| Command | Use |
652	|---|---|
653	| `entire graph search --query "<symptom summary>" --format agent --profile full --top-k 10 --max-context-bytes 24576` | Ranked source regions for the Pathologist's symptom summary |
654	| `cat failure.log \| entire graph explain` | Appends declarations of the symbols named in a stack trace or test failure |
655	| `entire graph impact --symbol <S> --depth 2 --exclude-tests --limit 15` | Blast radius: callers, callees, type consumers, data flows, related files |
656	| `entire graph neighbors --symbol <S> --relation CALLS --direction in --depth 1` | Direct callers (e.g. finding the retry wrapper) |
657	| `entire graph def <S>` | Declaration; for types, fields, methods and implementations (motif predicates) |
658	| `entire graph diff --base <sha> --head <sha>` | Entity-level change set (hypothesis scope, L4 drift) |
659	| `entire graph commit <rev>` | Entity changes in one commit, with estimated dependent counts |
660	| `entire graph checkpoint <CHECKPOINT_ID>` | Analyses the commit tied to an Entire checkpoint |
661	| `entire graph verify --test "<cmd>" --pre-edit-baseline` / `--record-baseline` | **G3:** which tests changed state |

### 4.3 Entire as episodic memory

#### 4.3.1 Setup and capture [V]

- `entire enable` MUST be run in every repository **before its first commit**: each host, `kintsugi-omega`, `kintsugi-antibodies` and `sabotage-log`. It installs the agent and git hooks.
- Checkpoints are created when the agent or a human makes a git commit (manual-commit strategy), or after each agent response (auto-commit strategy).
- Entire **never commits to the active branch**. Session metadata lives on the `entire/checkpoints/v1` branch.
- Each checkpoint captures:
  - the full transcript (prompts and responses);
  - file changes;
  - tool calls (commands run, files read);
  - token usage and timestamps;
  - sub-agents spawned through Claude Code's Task tool, as nested sessions.
- **Strategy choice.** Surgeons use the manual-commit strategy, so **one checkpoint corresponds to exactly one hypothesis attempt**. The proof bundle can then list every attempt, including failed ones.

#### 4.3.2 Recovering intent (why the code exists)

```
1. Localize      entire graph search / explain / impact     → file:line ranges + symbols
2. Blame         git blame -L <range> --porcelain           → commit SHAs
3. Map           commit → Entire checkpoint                  [A: read checkpoint metadata on
                                                              entire/checkpoints/v1; fallback:
                                                              `entire explain` on the commit [V]]
4. Explain       entire explain <checkpoint|commit>          → session transcript summary
5. Extract       Archivist (Opus) → Intent Record (below); every clause MUST cite a verbatim quote
6. Verify        Auditor checks each quote appears verbatim in the checkpoint transcript (G5 precondition)
```

```yaml
intent_record:
  checkpoint: "ck_7f3a…"              # Entire checkpoint id
  commit: "c0ffee1…"
  session: "claude-code:…"            # agent session that authored the change
  stated_goal: "Refactor retry logic for readability"
  behavioral_contract:
    - clause: "No behavior change intended"
      quote: "…keep behavior identical, this is purely a readability refactor…"   # verbatim, ≤300 chars
  confidence: 0.86
```

Requiring quotes is the anti-hallucination rule. A contract clause without a verbatim quote is dropped.

#### 4.3.3 Bisecting across checkpoints

When the replay cassette passes at an older commit, the incident is a **regression**, and the Archivist runs:

```bash
git bisect start <bad_sha> <good_sha>
git bisect run kintsugi replay --cassette cas/INC-0042.yaml --seeds 3   # exit 0 = good, 1 = bad
```

Each bisect step is annotated with its Entire checkpoint. The output is the **first bad checkpoint**: the exact AI session, and therefore the exact prompt, that introduced the regression.

#### 4.3.4 Rewind and resume

- Rewind:
  - `entire checkpoint rewind --list` lists rewind points as JSON;
  - `entire checkpoint rewind --to <id>` restores to one of them;
  - older builds use `entire rewind`;
  - `--logs-only` restores logs without touching the working tree.
- `--reset` is destructive and MUST NOT be used in autonomous mode.
- `entire resume <branch>` checks out the branch and restores the latest checkpointed session metadata [V]. It is used on the L2 recovery path for in-place sessions.
- **Honest scope.** Surgeons work in disposable worktrees, so rewinding a failed hypothesis means *discard the worktree and keep its checkpoint as evidence*. In-place rewinds are used by long-lived sessions: the Immunologist's refinement sessions and L2 orphan recovery.

### 4.4 Entire's entire-graph as the body map [V]

entire-graph is an Entire CLI plugin (`entire graph …`). It parses the repository locally with tree-sitter, never sends code to a model or service, maps files, symbols and relations (callers, callees, type usage), and uses limited git history to find files that change together.

#### 4.4.1 Per-repository setup

| Command | Purpose in Omega |
|---|---|
| `entire graph init-agents --repo .` | Writes `.entire/graph-agent.md` and managed blocks in `AGENTS.md` and `CLAUDE.md`, so every Surgeon's Claude Code session uses the graph automatically |
| `entire graph index` | Builds the committed-tree cache before batches of `--head` queries |
| `entire graph capabilities --json` | Lists supported semantic languages and **relation types**. The motif language MUST only use relations listed here. |
| `entire graph doctor --json` | Health check, run in the Watchdog's checks |

#### 4.4.2 Localisation, impact and change analysis

| Command | Use |
|---|---|
| `entire graph search --query "<symptom summary>" --format agent --profile full --top-k 10 --max-context-bytes 24576` | Ranked source regions for the Pathologist's symptom summary |

| `entire graph impact --symbol <S> --depth 2 --exclude-tests --limit 15` | Blast radius: callers, callees, type consumers, data flows, related files |
| `entire graph neighbors --symbol <S> --relation CALLS --direction in --depth 1` | Direct callers (e.g. finding the retry wrapper) |
| `entire graph def <S>` | Declaration; for types, fields, methods and implementations (motif predicates) |
| `entire graph diff --base <sha> --head <sha>` | Entity-level change set (hypothesis scope, L4 drift) |
| `entire graph commit <rev>` | Entity changes in one commit, with estimated dependent counts |
| `entire graph checkpoint <CHECKPOINT_ID>` | Analyses the commit tied to an Entire checkpoint |
| `entire graph verify --test "<cmd>" --pre-edit-baseline` / `--record-baseline` | **G3:** which tests changed state |

Getting Started:
  To get started with Entire CLI, run 'entire enable' to enable
  session tracking in your repository, then 'entire agent add <name>'
  to install hooks for a specific agent. For more information, visit:

Environment Variables:

Usage:

  entire [command]

Entire Setup:

  clean                      Clean up Entire session data
  configure                  Update Entire settings in the current repository
  disable                    Disable Entire in current repository
  doctor                     Diagnose and fix session issues

  plugin                     Manage Entire plugins (install, list, upgrade, search, remove)
  status                     Show Entire status

  activity                   Show your activity overview

Manage Entire plugins.

Plugins are external executables named 'entire-<name>'. The CLI discovers
plugins on $PATH and from a per-user managed directory which is
auto-prepended to PATH at startup. The managed directory is, in order of
precedence:

download the platform's release asset (verified against the release's
checksums.txt when published). Discovery uses a git-synced plugin index;
see 'entire plugin search' and 'entire plugin index update'.

Usage:

  browse      Interactively browse the plugin index and install

  install     Install a plugin from the index, a git repository URL, or a local executable
  list        List plugins installed in the managed directory
  remove      Remove a plugin from the managed directory
  search      Search the plugin index
  upgrade     Upgrade remote-installed plugins to their newest tag

definition.name: mcp__aws-mcp__aws___run_script
definition.description:
Execute Python code in sandboxed environment with AWS API access via `call_boto3`. No network except `call_boto3`.

```python
async def call_boto3(
    *,
    service_name: str,
    operation_name: str,
    region_name: str | None = None,
    params: dict | None = None,
) -> dict: ...
```

``operation_name`` MUST be the PascalCase AWS API operation name (e.g. ``ListBuckets``,
``GetTable``, ``StartQueryExecution``). Do not use the snake_case boto3 method name
(``list_buckets``, ``get_table``); exact matches are corrected only as a runtime fallback.

Response includes `api_calls` list—verify APIs ran before trusting `return_value`.

REQUIRED PATTERNS:
- Return `result={...}` then `result` alone as final expression
- Call each API once; results auto-paginate
- Return ALL resources—missing one is wrong
- Return raw data fields; let LLM judge thresholds
- Use `asyncio.gather(*[...])` with `return_exceptions=True` for reads; let mutations raise

⚠️ LIST→DESCRIBE: List* returns only names/ARNs. Use Get*/Describe* for attributes.

⚠️ CONTENTS vs CONTAINER: "empty buckets"→ListObjects; "records"→Scan; "X configured"→Get*Configuration.

RULES:
1. SELF-CONTAINED: Discover resources inside script.
2. ALL-REGIONS: DescribeRegions→gather per region.
3. PERMISSIONS: All policies ONE script. `bucket`≠`bucket/*`. Report YES/PARTIAL/NO.

PRE-IMPORTED: asyncio, collections, csv, dataclasses, datetime, decimal, enum, fractions, functools, itertools, json, math, re, statistics, string, time, typing, uuid, ClientError, io.StringIO, io.BytesIO.

BUILTIN MODULES: AWS teams provide higher-level functions for complex jobs. Find out more with:

```python
import aws_mcp
help(aws_mcp)
```

To search for available functions:

```python
await aws_mcp.search_functions("search query in natural language")
```

=== init-agents help ===
Install the coding-agent guide into AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md

Usage:
  entire graph init-agents [--repo path]

Writes the operating guide into a project's AGENTS.md and CLAUDE.md so any coding agent working in the repo knows to locate code with the graph before broad grep/read exploration.

Flags:
  --repo <path>   Repository to install into (default: current repo)

Examples:
  entire graph init-agents --repo .

#### 4.4.3 Snapshot export and the motif engine

```bash
entire graph snapshot --format compact-ndjson --worktree > graph/ledger@<sha>.ndjson
entire graph edges --relation CALLS --format ndjson --worktree > graph/ledger.calls.ndjson
entire graph snapshot-query --input graph/ledger@<sha>.ndjson     # cached queries, no rebuild
```

```python
import json
import networkx as nx
from networkx.algorithms.isomorphism import DiGraphMatcher

def load_snapshot(path: str) -> nx.DiGraph:
    """Collapse the multi-relation graph into a DiGraph whose edges carry a set of relation types.
    Record field names are [A] until checked against real compact-ndjson output (spike A9)."""
    G = nx.DiGraph()
    for line in open(path, encoding="utf-8"):
        rec = json.loads(line)
        if rec.get("type") == "symbol":
            G.add_node(rec["id"], **rec)
        elif rec.get("type") == "relation":
            u, v, rel = rec["from"], rec["to"], rec["relation"]
            if G.has_edge(u, v):
                G[u][v]["rels"].add(rel)
            else:
                G.add_edge(u, v, rels={rel})
    return G

def match_motif(G: nx.DiGraph, motif: nx.DiGraph, predicates) -> list[dict]:
    node_match = lambda g, m: all(predicates[p](g) for p in m.get("pred", [])) and g.get("kind") == m["kind"]
    edge_match = lambda g, m: m["rel"] in g["rels"]
    gm = DiGraphMatcher(G, motif, node_match=node_match, edge_match=edge_match)
    return list(gm.subgraph_monomorphisms_iter())   # monomorphism: extra edges in G are allowed
```

**Motif language.**

```yaml
motif:
  nodes:
    W: {kind: function, pred: [is_retry_wrapper]}
    F: {kind: function}
    S: {kind: class, pred: [has_mutable_accumulator]}
    T: {kind: function, pred: [is_side_effecting]}          # added by the L3 refinement (§6.7)
  edges:
    - [W, F, CALLS]
    - [F, S, CALLS]          # constructor call S.__init__ (relation name per `capabilities --json`)
    - [F, T, CALLS]          # added by the L3 refinement
  negative: []               # optional forbidden sub-patterns (immune tolerance)
```

**Predicates** are computed per node:
- `is_retry_wrapper`: decorator or call-site heuristics (`tenacity.retry`, `backoff.on_exception`, names matching `retry*`) confirmed with `entire graph def`.
- `has_mutable_accumulator`: the class has list, dict or set fields mutated in its methods, judged from `def` output plus a Haiku classifier.
- `is_side_effecting`: the function's transitive callees include a tool annotated `side_effect: true` in the host's tool registry, or an HTTP POST, PUT or DELETE.

**Motif validation** (required before an antibody is admitted):
1. It **matches** the origin host's graph *before* the fix.
2. It does **not** match the origin host's graph *after* the fix.
3. Precision on the healthy fleet is at or above 0.9 [I]. A match on a host known to be healthy for that pathogen counts as a false positive.

# entire-graph — instructions for coding agents (follow directly)

You have a deterministic local code graph: `entire graph` (functions, classes, methods,
types, routes + call/inheritance relations; no network). These instructions are FOR YOU, the
agent reading this file. Use the graph to narrow exploration without trading away correctness.

## The workflow (mandatory for locate/fix/change tasks)

Your FIRST action on any task that requires finding code must be ONE search:

    entire graph search --repo . --profile full --query "<the task or bug in one sentence>"

Then open the top hit's file with your file-read tool (pass a line range around the reported
line), inspect enough surrounding behavior to justify the change, and make the smallest complete
edit. Treat graph output as evidence, not an oracle.

## Hard rules

1. SEARCH FIRST — never grep/find/cat to locate code before you have searched.
2. READ focused source around the result. Widen the check when aliases, generated code, dynamic
   dispatch, or related implementations could matter.

6. Prefer precise queries and line ranges, but never trade resolution for fewer turns.
7. Feature-detect before relying on semantic relations:
       entire graph capabilities --json

## When NOT to use the graph

If the task already names the exact file and it is small, just read it — the graph saves tokens
by eliminating exploration; when there is nothing to explore, skip it.

---
name: msix-appdata-virtualization
description: Claude desktop app is MSIX-packaged; writes to %APPDATA%/%LOCALAPPDATA% from its sessions are redirected to the package LocalCache, breaking uv junctions and hiding entire plugins from normal terminals
metadata:
  type: project
---

The Claude desktop app on this machine runs as MSIX package `Claude_pzs8sxrjxfjjc`. Any tool run from a Claude session that writes under `%APPDATA%` or `%LOCALAPPDATA%` actually writes to `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Packages\Claude_pzs8sxrjxfjjc\LocalCache\{Roaming,Local}\...`. `%USERPROFILE%\.local\bin` is NOT virtualized.

Observed 2026-10-11:
- `uv python install 3.12` fails with "Missing expected target directory for Python minor version link". The junction `cpython-3.12-windows-x86_64-none` targets the real (empty) `%APPDATA%\uv\python\...` path. It also leaves a broken `~/.local/bin/python3.12.exe` trampoline, which was deleted. The 3.12.14 interpreter itself works via `uv run`/`uv python find` inside Claude sessions.
- `entire plugin install graph` landed in the virtualized `LocalCache\Local\entire\plugins\bin\entire-graph.exe`, so a regular terminal won't see `entire graph`.

**Why:** Tooling installed from Claude sessions must also work from normal terminals, git hooks, and spawned headless `claude -p` Surgeons.
**How to apply:** Recommended fix (pending user approval, needs an app restart): set user env vars `UV_PYTHON_INSTALL_DIR` and `ENTIRE_PLUGIN_DIR` to non-AppData paths under `%USERPROFILE%\.local\share\...`, then reinstall. See [[entire-checkpoint-turn-boundary]].

content.text:
Pre-Stage 1 is mostly done. Commit `05790aa` is pushed to `origin main` and the tree is clean, but the checkpoint check in step 4 failed: Entire made no checkpoint for that commit.

## Verification table

| # | Check | Result | Evidence |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1a | `entire` on PATH | ✅ | `~/.local/bin/entire` → Entire CLI 0.11.4 |
| 1b | Hooks active | ✅ | `entire status`: Enabled · Claude Code · this session `7e998687…` listed as active; 4 git hooks installed |
| 2a | Plugin name | ✅ | Official index entry is `graph`, from `entireio/entire-graph` |
| 2b | Install | ✅ | `graph` v0.4.0, `entire plugin doctor`: all healthy |
| 2c | `graph version --json` | ✅ | `{"provider":"entire-graph","version":"v0.4.0"}` |
| 2d | `graph capabilities --json` | ✅ | 30 relation types; Python is a semantic language |
| 2e | `graph doctor --json` | ✅ | `no_egress: true`, all network features off |
| 2f | `init-agents` | ✅ | Wrote [.entire/graph-agent.md](.entire/graph-agent.md), [CLAUDE.md](CLAUDE.md), [AGENTS.md](AGENTS.md) (guidance blocks only) |
| 3a | `uv python install 3.12` | ⚠️ | Downloaded 3.12.14, then failed on the version-link step (see issue 2). The interpreter itself works. |
| 3b | `uv python pin 3.12` | ✅ | [.python-version](.python-version) = `3.12`; `uv run` → Python 3.12.14 |
| 3c | Chocolatey shim | ✅ left alone | Only warns in the full `uv python list` scan; no warning in `find`/`run`/`venv` |
| 4a | Commit and push | ✅ | `05790aa`, 4 files, `e050b1e..05790aa main -> main` |
| 4b | Checkpoint ref | ❌ | No `Entire-Checkpoint` trailer; `git show-ref` has only `main` and `origin/main`; `entire checkpoint list`: 0 |

## Issues

**1. No checkpoint for `05790aa`.** The hooks ran at commit and push, but `entire session current` shows `turns: 0, checkpoints: 0`. Entire saves a turn's changes when the turn ends, and I committed in the middle of this session's first turn. Every change also came from a shell command (`init-agents`, `uv python pin`), so Entire may have had nothing to attribute to the session. The commit is pushed, so I won't amend it. From Stage 1 on, I'll check after every commit that it has the trailer and that the `entire/checkpoints/v1` ref exists. This matters for the spec, because §4.3.1 depends on one checkpoint per attempt.

**2. The Claude app redirects AppData writes.** This desktop app runs in a Windows app sandbox (`Claude_pzs8sxrjxfjjc`). Anything it writes under `%APPDATA%` or `%LOCALAPPDATA%` actually lands in that sandbox's private folder. That caused two problems:
- uv's version link points at the real `%APPDATA%` path, which is empty, so the install errors out. It also left a broken `~/.local/bin/python3.12.exe` on PATH, which I deleted.
- `entire-graph.exe` landed in the sandbox folder too. Inside Claude sessions everything works, but `entire graph` won't be found from a normal terminal.

The fix is to set two user environment variables to folders outside AppData, restart the app, and reinstall: `UV_PYTHON_INSTALL_DIR` and `ENTIRE_PLUGIN_DIR`, both under `%USERPROFILE%\.local\share\…`. That is a lasting change to your machine, so I haven't made it.

**3. Spec drift to fix in Stage 1:**
- **Wrong command names in §4.3.4 and Appendix D:** Entire 0.11.4 has no `rewind` command anywhere. `entire explain` is now `entire checkpoint explain`, and `entire resume` is now `entire session resume`. The rewind and L2 recovery paths need a quick test before we rely on them.
- **Unverified step in §4.3.2 can go:** a new experimental command, `entire why <file>:<line>`, gives the commit, checkpoint, prompt and session behind a line. It could replace the unverified step 3 (commit → checkpoint) in §4.3.2.
- **Motif rules in §4.4.3 need two fixes:**
  - For Python, constructor calls show up as `CONSTRUCTS`, not `CALLS`, so the edge `[F, S, CALLS]` (line 711) should be `[F, S, CONSTRUCTS]`.
  - Python has no `READS_FIELD`, `WRITES_FIELD` or `ACCESSES` relations, so `has_mutable_accumulator` can't use field-write edges. It has to rely on `def` output plus the classifier.
- Every `entire graph` command the spec uses exists in v0.4.0.

I saved issues 1–3 to project memory.

## Decisions before Stage 1
1. **Environment fix:** should I set `UV_PYTHON_INSTALL_DIR` and `ENTIRE_PLUGIN_DIR` and reinstall? You'd need to restart the app afterwards.
2. **Checkpoint test:** should the first Stage 1 commit be the test, or do you want a small commit first just to prove a checkpoint ref gets created and synced?

I'm stopping here until you give the Stage 1 go-ahead.

The Claude desktop app on this machine runs as MSIX package `Claude_pzs8sxrjxfjjc`. Any tool run from a Claude session that writes under `%APPDATA%` or `%LOCALAPPDATA%` actually writes to `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Packages\Claude_pzs8sxrjxfjjc\LocalCache\{Roaming,Local}\...`. `%USERPROFILE%\.local\bin` is NOT virtualized.

content.content:
entire checkpoint explain — Explain a session, commit, or checkpoint
Explain provides human-readable context about sessions, commits, and checkpoints.

Use this command to understand what happened during agent-driven development,
either for self-review or to understand a teammate's work.

By default, shows checkpoints on the current branch. Pass a checkpoint ID or
commit SHA as a positional argument to explain a specific item, or use flags.

Viewing specific items:
  entire checkpoint explain <id-or-sha>           Auto-detects checkpoint ID or commit SHA
  entire checkpoint explain --checkpoint <id>     Force interpretation as checkpoint ID
  entire checkpoint explain --commit <ref>        Force interpretation as commit ref

Checkpoints in another repo:
  entire checkpoint explain <id> --repo gh/owner/name
  entire checkpoint explain <id> --repo et/project/repo
                 Explain a checkpoint owned by another repository — the
                 drill-down for a cross-repo 'entire search' hit. Reads it from
                 that repo's Entire API; nothing is written to this repo.
                 Needs a full checkpoint ID (positional or --checkpoint) and a
                 checkpoint that has been pushed.

Filtering the list view:
  --session      Filter checkpoints by session ID (or prefix)

Output verbosity levels (when explaining a specific item):
  Default:         Detailed view with scoped prompts (ID, session, tokens, intent, prompts, files)
  --short          Summary only (ID, session, timestamp, tokens, intent)
  --full           Parsed full transcript (all prompts/responses from entire session)
  --raw-transcript Raw transcript file (JSONL format)

Machine-readable export modes (additive surface for external consumers):
  --json           Metadata-only JSON. Lists checkpoints when no target is given;
                   emits a single checkpoint envelope when a target is supplied,
                   including its subagent task records under "tasks".
                   Transcript bytes are NEVER embedded in the JSON envelope.
  --transcript     Stream stored checkpoint transcript bytes (JSONL) to stdout
                   for the selected session. Same bytes as --raw-transcript
                   while checkpoints v1 is the checkpoint store.
=== why help ===
Explain the commit, checkpoint, prompt, and session behind a file or line.

Target a specific line with <file>:12 or the --line flag.

Usage:
  entire why <file>[:line] [flags]

Examples:
  entire why src/auth.go:42
  entire why src/auth.go:42 --json

Flags:
  -h, --help          help for why
      --json          Output explanation as JSON
      --line string   Explain a specific line, for example 12 (same as <file>:12)

Global Flags:
      --context name   Act as this saved login name for this command only — including the git and agent processes it spawns — instead of the active context (entire auth contexts lists them)

---
name: entire-checkpoint-turn-boundary
description: How to get an Entire 0.11.4 checkpoint from a Claude commit on Windows (turn boundary + ENTIRE_TEST_TTY=0 hang fix), plus CLI drift vs Blueprint spec
metadata:
  type: project
---

Verified 2026-10-11. Commit 7745ee6 got checkpoint `01M4MSF9Q8JSKGD3RBEZB0XR1M`, synced to origin. It was the first commit with a checkpoint. The earlier 05790aa has none.

Recipe that works:
1. Edit files in turn N with Edit/Write. The Stop hook saves a shadow branch `entire/<base>-<hash>` ("checkpoint saved", modified_files).
2. Commit in turn N+1 with `ENTIRE_TEST_TTY=0 git commit ...`. Without it, `prepare-commit-msg` on Windows opens CONIN$ and blocks forever on an invisible "Link this commit to session context?" prompt. The hook's stderr goes to /dev/null, so nothing is shown. With it, the trailer is added automatically ("agent commit trailer added"). Use the same env var on `git push` (pre-push syncs refs).
3. If a commit hangs, kill git.exe FIRST (aborts the commit), then the hook processes. Killing only the hook makes `|| true` finish the commit without a trailer.

Facts:
- Default backend is per-checkpoint refs `refs/entire/checkpoints/<2-char>/<ULID>`, NOT the `entire/checkpoints/v1` branch the spec assumes (that branch is the legacy `--checkpoint-backend branch`).
- Checkpoint scope = everything since the last condensed checkpoint. `explain`'s "Intent" and `why`'s "Prompt" show the FIRST prompt in scope, not the turn that edited the line. For §4.3.2 Intent Records, select the turn by `turn_id` or the Edit tool call.
- Built-in redaction replaced the messaging token and account/org UUID lines with REDACTED even with 0 configured rules. Email and benign env vars remain. Transcripts are pushed to origin with the code.

**Why:** The spec (§4.3.1, §7) requires one checkpoint per commit or hypothesis attempt. Headless Surgeons on Windows will hang at commit without the env var.
**How to apply:** Proposed (awaiting user OK): put `ENTIRE_TEST_TTY=0` in the `.claude/settings.json` `env` block. Verify the trailer plus `git show-ref | grep refs/entire/` after every commit.

CLI drift in Entire 0.11.4 vs Blueprint §4.3.4/App D: no rewind command; `entire explain` → `entire checkpoint explain`; `entire resume` → `entire session resume`; `entire why <file>:<line>` exists. entire-graph v0.4.0: Python constructor calls = CONSTRUCTS; no READS_FIELD/WRITES_FIELD/ACCESSES/IMPLEMENTS for Python. See [[msix-appdata-virtualization]].

content.text:
The checkpoint chain works end to end: commit `7745ee6` is pushed with a checkpoint, and `entire why` traces the new `CLAUDE.md` line back to it. It only worked after I found and worked around a Windows hang in Entire's commit hook.

## Verification

| Check | Result | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| Commit and push | ✅ | `7745ee6`, pushed `05790aa..7745ee6 main -> main` |
| `Entire-Checkpoint` trailer | ✅ | `Entire-Checkpoint: 01M4MSF9Q8JSKGD3RBEZB0XR1M` |
| Local ref | ✅ | `refs/entire/checkpoints/1M/01M4MSF9Q8JSKGD3RBEZB0XR1M` → `025abdd` |
| Synced to `origin` | ✅ | Push printed `Pushing 1 checkpoint ref(s) to origin... done`; `ls-remote` shows the same ref and object |
| `entire checkpoint list` | ✅ | 1 checkpoint, linked to `7745ee6` |
| Attribution | ✅ | 10 of 10 lines credited to the agent, 1 file (`CLAUDE.md`) |
| `checkpoint explain` | ✅ | Session `7e998687`, model `claude-opus-5-5`, files `[CLAUDE.md]` |
| `why CLAUDE.md:12` | ✅ | `[AI] by Claude Code · claude-opus-5-5 · checkpoint 01M4MSF9… · session 7e998687 · commit 7745ee6b` |

## What went wrong, and the workaround
**The commit hung.** On Windows, Entire's pre-commit hook asks "Link this commit to session context?" on a console window that Claude's commands can't see, then waits forever for an answer. The hook also hides its error output, so nothing showed up.
- I aborted that first attempt cleanly. I stopped `git commit` before the hook, because stopping only the hook would have let the commit finish **without** the trailer.
- Entire has an undocumented variable, `ENTIRE_TEST_TTY=0`, that skips the question and links the commit automatically. I set it for this one commit and push only, so nothing about your setup has changed permanently.
- This affects every commit Claude makes here, including the spec's headless Surgeons on Windows.

## Other findings
- **Checkpoint storage differs from the spec.** Entire 0.11.4 stores each checkpoint as its own ref (`refs/entire/checkpoints/<xx>/<id>`). The `entire/checkpoints/v1` branch in §4.3.1 is a legacy option, so §4.3.2 step 3 and the proof bundle should read these refs instead.
- **"Intent" shows the wrong prompt.** Because `05790aa` never got a checkpoint, this one covers both turns. For §4.3.2 intent records, the Archivist (the spec's intent-recovery role) should pick the turn that actually made the edit instead of trusting that field.
- **Redaction worked.** The checkpoint transcript includes an environment dump I printed while debugging. Entire's built-in redaction replaced the session token and account/org IDs with `REDACTED`. What's left is your email (already public as the commit author), a process ID and an install path. Checkpoint transcripts are pushed alongside the code, so they are exactly as public as the repo.

content.text:
# Update Config Skill

Modify Claude Code configuration by updating settings.json files.

## When Hooks Are Required (Not Memory)

If the user wants something to happen automatically in response to an EVENT, they need a **hook** configured in settings.json. Memory/preferences cannot trigger automated actions.

**These require hooks:**
- "Before compacting, ask me what to preserve" → PreCompact hook
- "After writing files, run prettier" → PostToolUse hook with Write|Edit matcher
- "When I run bash commands, log them" → PreToolUse hook with Bash matcher
- "Always run tests after code changes" → PostToolUse hook

**Hook events:** PreToolUse, PostToolUse, PreCompact, PostCompact, Stop, Notification, SessionStart

## CRITICAL: Read Before Write

**Always read the existing settings file before making changes.** Merge new settings with existing ones - never replace the entire file.

## CRITICAL: Use AskUserQuestion for Ambiguity

When the user's request is ambiguous, use AskUserQuestion to clarify:
- Which settings file to modify (user/project/local)
- Whether to add to existing arrays or replace them
- Specific values when multiple options exist

## Decision: /config command vs Direct Edit

**Suggest the `/config` slash command** for these simple settings:
- `theme`, `editorMode`, `verbose`, `model`
- `language`, `alwaysThinkingEnabled`
- `permissions.defaultMode`

**Edit settings.json directly** for:
- Hooks (PreToolUse, PostToolUse, etc.)
- Complex permission rules (allow/deny arrays)
- Environment variables
- MCP server configuration
- Plugin configuration

## Workflow

1. **Clarify intent** - Ask if the request is ambiguous
2. **Read existing file** - Use Read tool on the target settings file
3. **Merge carefully** - Preserve existing settings, especially arrays
4. **Edit file** - Use Edit tool (if file doesn't exist, ask user to create it first)
5. **Confirm** - Tell user what was changed

## Merging Arrays (Important!)

When adding to permission arrays or hook arrays, **merge with existing**, don't replace:

**WRONG** (replaces existing permissions):
```json
{ "permissions": { "allow": ["Bash(npm *)"] } }
```

**RIGHT** (preserves existing + adds new):
```json
{
  "permissions": {
    "allow": [
      "Bash(git *)",      // existing
      "Edit(.claude)",    // existing
      "Bash(npm *)"       // new
    ]
  }
}
```

## Settings File Locations

Choose the appropriate file based on scope:

| File | Scope | Git | Use For |
|------|-------|-----|---------|
| `~/.claude/settings.json` | Global | N/A | Personal preferences for all projects |
| `.claude/settings.json` | Project | Commit | Team-wide hooks, permissions, plugins |
| `.claude/settings.local.json` | Project | Gitignore | Personal overrides for this project |

Settings load in order: user → project → local (later overrides earlier).

## Settings Schema Reference

### Permissions
```json
{
  "permissions": {
    "allow": ["Bash(npm *)", "Edit(.claude)", "Read"],
    "deny": ["Bash(rm -rf *)"],
    "ask": ["Edit(//etc/*)"],
    "defaultMode": "default" | "plan" | "acceptEdits" | "dontAsk",
    "additionalDirectories": ["/extra/dir"]
  }
}
```

**Permission Rule Syntax:**
- Exact match: `"Bash(npm run test)"`
- Prefix wildcard: `"Bash(git *)"` - matches `git`, `git status`, `git commit`, etc.
- Tool only: `"Read"` - allows all Read operations
- File paths: `"Edit(src/**)"` - path rules in `permissions` use `Edit(path)` for every file-writing tool (Write, Edit, NotebookEdit) and `Read(path)` for reads. `Write(path)`, `NotebookEdit(path)` and `Glob(path)` rules are not matched by file permission checks. Bare tool names (`"Write"`), deny/ask `Tool(param:value)` rules and hook `if` conditions still use each tool's own name

### Environment Variables
```json
{
  "env": {
    "DEBUG": "true",
    "MY_API_KEY": "value"
  }
}
```

### Model & Agent
```json
{
  "model": "sonnet",  // or "fable", "opus", "haiku", full model ID
  "agent": "agent-name",
  "alwaysThinkingEnabled": true
}
```

### Attribution (Commits & PRs)
```json
{
  "attribution": {
    "commit": "Custom commit trailer text",
    "pr": "Custom PR description text"
  }
}
```
Set `commit` or `pr` to empty string `""` to hide that attribution. To hide all of it, set both to `""` and also set `"sessionUrl": false`. Write this object form, not `"attribution": false`: older Claude Code versions reject true or false here and then skip the whole settings file.

### MCP Server Management
```json
{
  "enableAllProjectMcpServers": true,
  "enabledMcpjsonServers": ["server1", "server2"],
  "disabledMcpjsonServers": ["blocked-server"]
}
```

### Plugins
```json
{
  "enabledPlugins": {
    "formatter@anthropic-tools": true
  }
}
```
Plugin syntax: `plugin-name@source` where source is `claude-code-marketplace`, `claude-plugins-official`, or `builtin`.

### Other Settings
- `language`: Preferred response language (e.g., "japanese")
- `cleanupPeriodDays`: Days to keep transcripts before automatic cleanup (default: 30; minimum 1)
- `respectGitignore`: Whether to respect .gitignore (default: true)
- `spinnerTipsEnabled`: Show tips in spinner
- `timeFormat`: Clock format for times shown in the UI: "auto" (default), "12-hour", "24-hour", "24-hour-utc", or a strftime pattern such as "%H:%M"
- `timeZone`: IANA time zone for times shown in the UI, e.g. "UTC" (default: system time zone)
- `spinnerVerbs`: Customize spinner verbs (`{ "mode": "append" | "replace", "verbs": [...] }`)
- `spinnerTipsOverride`: Override spinner tips (`{ "excludeDefault": true, "tips": ["Custom tip"] }`)
- `syntaxHighlightingDisabled`: Disable diff highlighting


## Hooks Configuration

Hooks run commands at specific points in Claude Code's lifecycle.

### Hook Structure
```json
{
  "hooks": {
    "EVENT_NAME": [
      {
        "matcher": "ToolName|OtherTool",
        "hooks": [
          {
            "type": "command",
            "command": "your-command-here",
            "timeout": 60,
            "statusMessage": "Running..."
          }
        ]
      }
    ]
  }
}
```

### Hook Events

| Event | Matcher | Purpose |
|-------|---------|---------|
| PermissionRequest | Tool name | Run before permission prompt |
| PreToolUse | Tool name | Run before tool, can block |
| PostToolUse | Tool name | Run after successful tool |
| PostToolUseFailure | Tool name | Run after tool fails |
| Notification | Notification type | Run on notifications |
| Stop | - | Run when Claude stops (including clear, resume, compact) |
| PreCompact | "manual"/"auto" | Before compaction |
| PostCompact | "manual"/"auto" | After compaction (receives summary) |
| UserPromptSubmit | - | When user submits |
| SessionStart | - | When session starts |

**Common tool matchers:** `Bash`, `Write`, `Edit`, `Read`, `Glob`, `Grep`

### Hook Types

**1. Command Hook** - Runs a shell command:
```json
{ "type": "command", "command": "prettier --write $FILE", "timeout": 30 }
```

**2. Prompt Hook** - Evaluates a condition with LLM:
```json
{ "type": "prompt", "prompt": "Is this safe? $ARGUMENTS" }
```
Only available for tool events: PreToolUse, PostToolUse, PermissionRequest.

**3. Agent Hook** - Runs an agent with tools:
```json
{ "type": "agent", "prompt": "Verify tests pass: $ARGUMENTS" }
```
Only available for tool events: PreToolUse, PostToolUse, PermissionRequest.

### Hook Input (stdin JSON)
```json
{
  "session_id": "abc123",
  "tool_name": "Write",
  "tool_input": { "file_path": "/path/to/file.txt", "content": "..." },
  "tool_response": { "success": true }  // PostToolUse only
}
```

### Hook JSON Output

Hooks can return JSON to control behavior:

```json
{
  "systemMessage": "Warning shown to user in UI",
  "continue": false,
  "stopReason": "Message shown when blocking",
  "suppressOutput": false,
  "decision": "block",
  "reason": "Explanation for decision",
  "hookSpecificOutput": {
    "hookEventName": "PostToolUse",
    "additionalContext": "Context injected back to model"
  }
}
```

**Fields:**
- `systemMessage` - Display a message to the user (all hooks)
- `continue` - Set to `false` to block/stop (default: true)
- `stopReason` - Message shown when `continue` is false
- `suppressOutput` - Hide stdout from transcript (default: false)
- `decision` - "block" for PostToolUse/Stop/UserPromptSubmit hooks (deprecated for PreToolUse, use hookSpecificOutput.permissionDecision instead)
- `reason` - Explanation for decision
- `hookSpecificOutput` - Event-specific output (must include `hookEventName`):
  - `additionalContext` - Text injected into model context
  - `permissionDecision` - "allow", "deny", or "ask" (PreToolUse only)
  - `permissionDecisionReason` - Reason for the permission decision (PreToolUse only)
  - `updatedInput` - Modified tool input (PreToolUse only)

### Common Patterns

**Auto-format after writes:**
```json
{
  "hooks": {
    "PostToolUse": [{
      "matcher": "Write|Edit",
      "hooks": [{
        "type": "command",
        "command": "jq -r '.tool_response.filePath // .tool_input.file_path' | { read -r f; prettier --write \"$f\"; } 2>/dev/null || true"
      }]
    }]
  }
}
```

**Log all bash commands:**
```json
{
  "hooks": {
    "PreToolUse": [{
      "matcher": "Bash",
      "hooks": [{
        "type": "command",
        "command": "jq -r '.tool_input.command' >> ~/.claude/bash-log.txt"
      }]
    }]
  }
}
```

**Stop hook that displays message to user:**

Command must output JSON with `systemMessage` field:
```bash
# Example command that outputs: {"systemMessage": "Session complete!"}
echo '{"systemMessage": "Session complete!"}'
```

**Run tests after code changes:**
```json
{
  "hooks": {
    "PostToolUse": [{
      "matcher": "Write|Edit",
      "hooks": [{
        "type": "command",
        "command": "jq -r '.tool_input.file_path // .tool_response.filePath' | grep -E '\\.(ts|js)$' && npm test || true"
      }]
    }]
  }
}
```


## Constructing a Hook (with verification)

Given an event, matcher, target file, and desired behavior, follow this flow. Each step catches a different failure class — a hook that silently does nothing is worse than no hook.

1. **Dedup check.** Read the target file. If a hook already exists on the same event+matcher, show the existing command and ask: keep it, replace it, or add alongside.

2. **Construct the command for THIS project — don't assume.** The hook receives JSON on stdin. Build a command that:
   - Extracts any needed payload safely — use `jq -r` into a quoted variable or `{ read -r f; ... "$f"; }`, NOT unquoted `| xargs` (splits on spaces)
   - Invokes the underlying tool the way this project runs it (npx/bunx/yarn/pnpm? Makefile target? globally-installed?)
   - Skips inputs the tool doesn't handle (formatters often have `--ignore-unknown`; if not, guard by extension)
   - Stays RAW for now — no `|| true`, no stderr suppression. You'll wrap it after the pipe-test passes.

3. **Pipe-test the raw command.** Synthesize the stdin payload the hook will receive and pipe it directly:
   - `Pre|PostToolUse` on `Write|Edit`: `echo '{"tool_name":"Edit","tool_input":{"file_path":"<a real file from this repo>"}}' | <cmd>`
   - `Pre|PostToolUse` on `Bash`: `echo '{"tool_name":"Bash","tool_input":{"command":"ls"}}' | <cmd>`
   - `Stop`/`UserPromptSubmit`/`SessionStart`: most commands don't read stdin, so `echo '{}' | <cmd>` suffices

   Check exit code AND side effect (file actually formatted, test actually ran). If it fails you get a real error — fix (wrong package manager? tool not installed? jq path wrong?) and retest. Once it works, wrap with `2>/dev/null || true` (unless the user wants a blocking check).

4. **Write the JSON.** Merge into the target file (schema shape in the "Hook Structure" section above). If this creates `.claude/settings.local.json` for the first time, add it to .gitignore — the Write tool doesn't auto-gitignore it.

5. **Validate syntax + schema in one shot:**

   `jq -e '.hooks.<event>[] | select(.matcher == "<matcher>") | .hooks[] | select(.type == "command") | .command' <target-file>`

   Exit 0 + prints your command = correct. Exit 4 = matcher doesn't match. Exit 5 = malformed JSON or wrong nesting. A broken settings.json silently disables ALL settings from that file — fix any pre-existing malformation too.

6. **Prove the hook fires** — only for `Pre|PostToolUse` on a matcher you can trigger in-turn (`Write|Edit` via Edit, `Bash` via Bash). `Stop`/`UserPromptSubmit`/`SessionStart` fire outside this turn — skip to step 7.

   For a **formatter** on `PostToolUse`/`Write|Edit`: introduce a detectable violation via Edit (two consecutive blank lines, bad indentation, missing semicolon — something this formatter corrects; NOT trailing whitespace, Edit strips that before writing), re-read, confirm the hook **fixed** it. For **anything else**: temporarily prefix the command in settings.json with `echo "$(date) hook fired" >> /tmp/claude-hook-check.txt; `, trigger the matching tool (Edit for `Write|Edit`, a harmless `true` for `Bash`), read the sentinel file.

   **Always clean up** — revert the violation, strip the sentinel prefix — whether the proof passed or failed.

   **If proof fails but pipe-test passed and `jq -e` passed**: the settings watcher isn't watching `.claude/` — it only watches directories that had a settings file when this session started. The hook is written correctly. Tell the user to start a new session so the new settings load. You can't do this yourself.

7. **Handoff.** Tell the user the hook is live (or needs a new session per the watcher caveat), and that they can review, edit, or disable it later in the settings file you wrote. The UI only shows "Ran N hooks" if a hook errors or is slow — silent success is invisible by design.


## Example Workflows

### Adding a Hook

User: "Format my code after Claude writes it"

1. **Clarify**: Which formatter? (prettier, gofmt, etc.)
2. **Read**: `.claude/settings.json` (or create if missing)
3. **Merge**: Add to existing hooks, don't replace
4. **Result**:
```json
{
  "hooks": {
    "PostToolUse": [{
      "matcher": "Write|Edit",
      "hooks": [{
        "type": "command",
        "command": "jq -r '.tool_response.filePath // .tool_input.file_path' | { read -r f; prettier --write \"$f\"; } 2>/dev/null || true"
      }]
    }]
  }
}
```

### Adding Permissions

User: "Allow npm commands without prompting"

1. **Read**: Existing permissions
2. **Merge**: Add `Bash(npm *)` to allow array
3. **Result**: Combined with existing allows

### Environment Variables

User: "Set DEBUG=true"

1. **Decide**: User settings (global) or project settings?
2. **Read**: Target file
3. **Merge**: Add to env object
```json
{ "env": { "DEBUG": "true" } }
```

## Common Mistakes to Avoid

1. **Replacing instead of merging** - Always preserve existing settings
2. **Wrong file** - Ask user if scope is unclear
3. **Invalid JSON** - Validate syntax after changes
4. **Forgetting to read first** - Always read before write

## Troubleshooting Hooks

If a hook isn't running:
1. **Check the settings file** - Read ~/.claude/settings.json or .claude/settings.json
2. **Verify JSON syntax** - Invalid JSON silently fails
3. **Check the matcher** - Does it match the tool name? (e.g., "Bash", "Write", "Edit")
4. **Check hook type** - Is it "command", "prompt", or "agent"?
5. **Test the command** - Run the hook command manually to see if it works
6. **Use --debug** - Run `claude --debug` to see hook execution logs


## Full Settings JSON Schema

```json
{
  "$schema": "https://json-schema.org/draft/2020-12/schema",
  "type": "object",
  "properties": {
    "$schema": {
      "description": "JSON Schema reference for Claude Code settings",
      "type": "string"
    },
    "apiKeyHelper": {
      "description": "Path to a script that outputs authentication values",
      "type": "string"
    },
    "proxyAuthHelper": {
      "description": "Shell command that outputs a Proxy-Authorization header value (EAP)",
      "type": "string"
    },
    "awsCredentialExport": {
      "description": "Path to a script that exports AWS credentials",
      "type": "string"
    },
    "awsAuthRefresh": {
      "description": "Path to a script that refreshes AWS authentication",
      "type": "string"
    },
    "gcpAuthRefresh": {
      "description": "Command to refresh GCP authentication (e.g., gcloud auth application-default login)",
      "type": "string"
    },
    "processWrapper": {
      "description": "Corporate launcher argv prefix for the background-agent supervisor, the sessions and workers it hosts, and the other covered background processes listed in the Claude Code corporate-launcher documentation. Equivalent to the CLAUDE_CODE_PROCESS_WRAPPER environment variable, which takes precedence when set. Honored from managed settings, a --settings/SDK-supplied settings file, and user settings, in that precedence order; project and local settings are ignored.",
      "type": "string"
    },
    "policyHelper": {
      "description": "Executable that computes managed settings at startup. Honored only from admin-controlled policy sources.",
      "type": "object",
      "properties": {
        "path": {
          "description": "Absolute path to the helper executable",
          "type": "string"
        },
        "timeoutMs": {
          "type": "integer",
          "minimum": 1000,
          "maximum": 9007199254740991
        },
        "refreshIntervalMs": {
          "anyOf": [
            {
              "type": "number",
              "const": 0
            },
            {
              "type": "integer",
              "minimum": 60000,
              "maximum": 9007199254740991
            }
          ]
        }
      },
      "required": [
        "path"
      ]
    },
    "fileSuggestion": {
      "description": "Custom file suggestion configuration for @ mentions",
      "type": "object",
      "properties": {
        "type": {
          "type": "string",
          "const": "command"
        },
        "command": {
          "type": "string"
        }
      },
      "required": [
        "type",
        "command"
      ]
    },
    "respectGitignore": {
      "description": "Whether file picker should respect .gitignore files (default: true). Note: .ignore files are always respected.",
      "type": "boolean"
    },
    "cleanupPeriodDays": {
      "description": "Number of days to retain chat transcripts before automatic cleanup (default: 30). Minimum 1. Use a large value for long retention; use --no-session-persistence to disable transcript writes entirely.",
      "type": "integer",
      "exclusiveMinimum": 0,
      "maximum": 9007199254740991
    },
    "desktopSessionCleanupPeriodDays": {
      "description": "Retention ceiling in days for session transcripts created or last written by a desktop-host surface (Claude Desktop, Cowork), which are otherwise exempt from the cleanupPeriodDays sweep. 0 (the default) means no ceiling: such transcripts are kept until deleted another way. Unlike cleanupPeriodDays, 0 is allowed because this setting never disables writes — it only bounds an exemption from deletion. Verified 2026-10-11. Commit 7745ee6 got checkpoint `01M4MSF9Q8JSKGD3RBEZB0XR1M`, synced to origin. It was the first commit with a checkpoint. The earlier 05790aa has none.

Recipe that works:
1. Edit files in turn N with Edit/Write. The Stop hook saves a shadow branch `entire/<base>-<hash>` ("checkpoint saved", modified_files).
2. Commit in turn N+1 with `ENTIRE_TEST_TTY=0 git commit ...`. Without it, `prepare-commit-msg` on Windows opens CONIN$ and blocks forever on an invisible "Link this commit to session context?" prompt. The hook's stderr goes to /dev/null, so nothing is shown. With it, the trailer is added automatically ("agent commit trailer added"). Use the same env var on `git push` (pre-push syncs refs).
3. If a commit hangs, kill git.exe FIRST (aborts the commit), then the hook processes. Killing only the hook makes `|| true` finish the commit without a trailer.

Facts:
- Default backend is per-checkpoint refs `refs/entire/checkpoints/<2-char>/<ULID>`, NOT the `entire/checkpoints/v1` branch the spec assumes (that branch is the legacy `--checkpoint-backend branch`).
- Checkpoint scope = everything since the last condensed checkpoint. `explain`'s "Intent" and `why`'s "Prompt" show the FIRST prompt in scope, not the turn that edited the line. For §4.3.2 Intent Records, select the turn by `turn_id` or the Edit tool call.
- Built-in redaction replaced the messaging token and account/org UUID lines with REDACTED even with 0 configured rules. Email and benign env vars remain. Transcripts are pushed to origin with the code.

**Why:** The spec (§4.3.1, §7) requires one checkpoint per commit or hypothesis attempt. Headless Surgeons on Windows will hang at commit without the env var.
**How to apply:** Proposed (awaiting user OK): put `ENTIRE_TEST_TTY=0` in the `.claude/settings.json` `env` block. Verify the trailer plus `git show-ref | grep refs/entire/` after every commit.

CLI drift in Entire 0.11.4 vs Blueprint §4.3.4/App D: no rewind command; `entire explain` → `entire checkpoint explain`; `entire resume` → `entire session resume`; `entire why <file>:<line>` exists. entire-graph v0.4.0: Python constructor calls = CONSTRUCTS; no READS_FIELD/WRITES_FIELD/ACCESSES/IMPLEMENTS for Python. See [[msix-appdata-virtualization]].

The fresh remote now has the clean `main` and both checkpoints, and every ref matches local. The old un-scrubbed commits are deleted locally, so they can't be pushed again.

## Results

| Step | Result |
|---|---|
| 1. Delete backup ref | ✅ `refs/original/refs/heads/main` removed |
| 1. Expire reflogs and prune | ✅ All 5 pre-rewrite commits are gone locally (`88e16d3`, `e050b1e`, `05790aa`, `7745ee6`, `041ada4`); `git fsck` is clean |
| 2. Authorship on all refs | ✅ 9 commits on `main` plus the checkpoint refs; the only identity is `Surya Prasanth R <suryaprasanthcse@gmail.com>` |
| 2. Co-author / Anthropic check | ✅ 0 `Co-authored-by` lines, 0 Claude or Anthropic author/committer entries, 0 `noreply@anthropic.com` in commit messages |
| 3. `git push -u origin main` | ✅ `* [new branch] main -> main`, tracking set |
| 3. Checkpoint refs | ✅ Both are on the remote |
| 4. Remote state | ✅ `main` = `c299a26`, `01M4MSF9…` = `0eabc67`, `01M4MT4M…` = `d0227e3`, all matching local |
| 4. `entire checkpoint list` | ✅ 2 checkpoints, linked to `c299a26` and `3ea631e` |

## Things I handled along the way
- **I kept Entire's session state valid before pruning.** Entire still pointed at the pre-rewrite commit `041ada4`, and `filter-branch` never tells Entire about a rewrite. While the old objects still existed, I gave Entire the old-to-new commit mapping through its own rewrite hook. It updated the fields it uses to credit lines on the next commit. It left one bookkeeping field on `041ada4`; I'll check that the first Stage 1 commit still gets its checkpoint and line credit.
- **Your explicit checkpoint push was necessary.** Entire's push hook only sent the newer checkpoint, because it remembered the older one as already pushed to the old remote. Without your second push, `01M4MSF9…` would have been missing from GitHub.
- **Transcript text still mentions `noreply@anthropic.com`.** Each checkpoint's saved session log has 13 lines containing it, from my earlier commit commands. That's file content in Entire's own storage, not commit authorship. GitHub only builds its contributor list from commits on branches, so it isn't affected.

I've added the rewrite hook step and the explicit checkpoint push to memory. I'm stopping here until you've checked the GitHub page and give the Stage 1 go-ahead.

1	# Blueprint Omega — Master Specification
2	
3	## KINTSUGI‑Ω: An Immune System for AI Agents
4	
5	> *Kintsugi* is the Japanese craft of repairing broken pottery with gold, so that the repair is visible instead of hidden. Omega applies the same principle to AI agents. Every failure is repaired, every repair is proven, and every seam stays visible in neatlogs traces and Entire checkpoints.
6	
7	| Field | Value |
8	|---|---|
9	| Document | `Blueprint_Omega_Master.md` |
10	| Version | 1.0 — full-version design specification |
11	| Date | 2026‑10‑11 |
12	| Event | #neatHack, the AI agent hackathon run by neatlogs and powered by cfo.ai and Entire. Build: Oct 10–12, 2026. Submission window: Mon 12 Oct 2026, 7:00–11:55 PM IST (final cutoff on Discord). |
13	| Track | "Build an agent that works (literally)" (the only track) |
14	| Status | Design locked (full version). Implementation not started. |
15	| Lineage | Equilibrium (AEGIS‑ZERO) → Refined Equilibrium → KINTSUGI → KINTSUGI v2 → **Blueprint Omega** |
16	
17	---
18	
19	## Table of contents
20	
21	0. Reading guide and conventions
22	1. Executive summary
23	2. Strategic context: lineage, gap analysis, requirements traceability
24	3. Core mandate and biological paradigm (including Wright's-law economics)
25	4. The nervous system: neatlogs, Entire and cfo.ai integration mechanics
26	5. Architecture: planes, orchestrator, crew, memory, fleet, gates, statistics
27	6. The engineered failure cascade (L0–L5)
28	7. The un-fakeable proof matrix
29	8. Demo video script
30	9. Building-in-public plan
31	10. cfo.ai business plan
32	11. Technology stack
33	12. Repository layout
34	13. Assumptions, Day‑0 spikes and risks
35	14. Probability calibration and comparative matrix
36	15. Build roadmap
37	- Appendix A — Glossary
38	- Appendix B — Saboteur fault catalog
39	- Appendix C — neatlogs API surface used
40	- Appendix D — Entire command surface used
41	- Appendix E — Schemas
42	- Appendix F — Sources
43	
44	---
45	
46	## 0. Reading guide and conventions
47	
48	**Normative language.** MUST, MUST NOT, SHOULD, SHOULD NOT and MAY follow RFC 2119.
49	
50	**Evidence labels.** Every external interface and every number in this document carries one of these labels:
51	
52	| Label | Meaning |
53	|---|---|
54	| **[V]** | Verified: the interface appears in the vendor's public documentation or OpenAPI specification as of 2026‑10‑11. |
55	| **[A]** | Assumed: plausible but not yet verified. Each has a Day‑0 spike in §13. |
56	| **[I]** | Illustrative: a design target or worked example, **not a measured result**. [I] numbers MUST NOT appear as results in the submission. Replace them with measured values. |
57	
58	**Probability statement.** The full-build estimate in §14 (about 55% top‑3, about 30% 1st) is the *ceiling* for any entry under flawless execution. It is a judgement, not a guarantee, and it depends on a field nobody can observe. The realistic estimate for a build done inside the hackathon window is much lower (about 28% top‑3, about 10% 1st).
59	
60	**Notation.**
61	
62	| Symbol | Meaning |
63	|---|---|
64	| h ∈ H | A host: an AI agent under Omega's protection |
65	| τ, σ | A neatlogs trace and a span |
66	| φ(τ) | The failure signature of a trace |
67	| ι | An incident |
68	| a | An antibody |
69	| M_a, P_a | The structural motif and the learned preconditions of antibody a |
70	| G_h | The entire-graph code graph of host h |
71	| W | The autonomy window (default 24 h) |
72	| B_ι | The budget allocated to incident ι |
73	| GM_floor | The gross-margin floor from the cfo.ai model |
74	
75	---
76	
77	## 1. Executive summary
78	
79	Omega is an autonomous reliability system for a **fleet** of AI agents. It is modeled on the adaptive immune system, not on a single repair agent.
80	
81	- **It senses.** Every host's runs stream into neatlogs. Detections act as receptors, and alert webhooks act as the reflex arc.
82	- **It repairs.** A crew of specialised agents:
83	  - reproduces the failure deterministically;
84	  - finds the responsible code with entire-graph;
85	  - recovers *why that code exists* from the Entire checkpoint that created it;
86	  - repairs it in parallel git worktrees with headless Claude Code;
87	  - accepts a fix only when it passes eight gates. These include a statistically significant improvement on encrypted held-out tasks and an independent CI run.
88	- **It remembers.** Every verified repair is distilled into an **antibody**: a portable unit made of a neatlogs detection, a structural code motif, a repair recipe and a verification contract. When a failure recurs, Omega skips diagnosis. Cost per repair falls along a Wright's-law learning curve, which becomes a driver of gross margin in the cfo.ai model.
89	- **It prevents.** Antibody motifs are matched against the code graphs of hosts that have never failed. Where a motif matches, the failure is induced in a sandbox to prove the host is vulnerable, then fixed before it ever reaches production.
90	- **It heals itself.** Omega survives `kill -9` of its own workers and the loss of its webhook feed, through durable execution and reconciliation. It detects when one of its own fixes is wrong in production, reverts it, quarantines the antibody and learns the missing precondition.
91	- **It is governed by economics.** A cfo.ai unit-economics model decides:
92	  - every incident's budget;
93	  - the order of work (dollars at risk);
94	  - the size of every verification experiment;
95	  - when to switch from repair to a cheaper treatment, or escalate to a human.
96	- **It proves everything.**
97	  - Sabotage is sealed with a hash before injection.
98	  - Every incident is written to a hash-chained ledger.
99	  - Every commit inside the window is cryptographically attested and linked to an Entire checkpoint.
100	  - The strongest evidence comes from outside the team: maintainers of other teams' agents who chose to merge Omega's PRs.
101	
102	**One-line hook for the judges:** *"Nobody touched this code for 24 hours. N agents, M incidents, 0 human commits, and you can audit every one."* N and M are measured at submission time.
103	
104	---
105	
106	## 2. Strategic context
107	
108	### 2.1 Lineage
109	
110	| Version | Core idea | Limitation that led to the next version |
111	|---|---|---|
112	| Equilibrium (AEGIS‑ZERO) | Red/Blue dual-state security self-healing against a target service | We write the proof ourselves (a planted bug and local verification). The *target* fails, not the agent. The security-autofix lane is crowded. |
113	| Refined Equilibrium | Replay of real advisories; commit-reveal of the PoC; independent CI; gate-driven replanning | The sponsor tools are still only instrumentation. Its shape matches the most common example task ("Fix a GitHub issue"), so originality suffers. |
114	| KINTSUGI | An agent that repairs AI agents from neatlogs traces, preserving intent recovered from Entire checkpoints | Only one patient agent, which we built. The value is linear. |
115	| KINTSUGI v2 | A crew with a coordinator; tolerance for drift during a repair; context manifests | The proof is closed-world. Nothing compounds. There is no prevention. It only recovers from first-order failures. |
116	| **Blueprint Omega** | An immune system for a fleet: compounding antibodies, vaccination, second-order recovery, external proof, economic governance | Scope: about 4 engineer-weeks for the full build |
117	
118	### 2.2 Gap analysis: why KINTSUGI v2 capped at about 16% for 1st place
119	
120	**Decomposition.**
121	
122	```
123	P(1st) ≈ P(entry is in the top tier) × P(entry beats the other top-tier entries)
124	KINTSUGI v2:  ≈ 0.50 × 0.30 ≈ 0.15
125	Target:       ≈ 0.70 × 0.45 ≈ 0.31
126	```
127	
128	The second factor only moves when the entry has something **that no other top-tier entry has**. Better execution of the same idea does not move it.
129	
130	| Gap in v2 | Why it caps 1st place | Omega's answer |
131	|---|---|---|
132	| Closed-world proof | We author the patient, the failures and the verifier, so judges read it as "a well-made demo". | External proof: strangers merge our PRs (Repair Clinic), and judges trigger sealed sabotage themselves (Arena). |
133	| Linear value | Each repair costs the same, which makes it a services business with flat margins. | Antibodies compound: costs follow Wright's law, and every antibody protects every host. |
134	| Reactive only | It fixes failures only after they happen. | Vaccination: it fixes failures that have never occurred, in agents that have never failed. |
135	| First-order recovery only | It recovers from the patient's failures and its own failed attempts, but not from its own wrong fix reaching production. | L3: a canary SPRT detects the wrong fix, then Omega auto-reverts, quarantines the antibody and learns a precondition. |
136	| Hard to take in | Six roles and six gates, with no single shocking number. | "0 human commits in 24 h across N agents", verifiable by anyone with `kintsugi audit`. |
137	| Building in public was a side task | Posting happened next to the work instead of coming out of it. | The product is public and participatory: hourly ledger anchors, the Clinic, the Arena. |
138	
139	**What each sponsor's product implies its judges value.** This is inferred from what each company builds, not from anything the judges have said.
140	
141	- **neatlogs:** their Detections → Fixes loop closed all the way to *verified and never happens again*. neatlogs becomes the senses of an autonomous operator, not a dashboard someone has to watch. Their Fixes documentation lists dispatch to Cursor Cloud Agents only, with Claude Code "planned" [V]. Omega is a Claude Code dispatch target that also verifies the result.
142	- **Entire:** the history of AI-made changes becomes **machine-usable**. It serves as the repair memory (intent-preserving fixes) and as the notary that proves autonomy.
143	- **Orchestrator.inc:** durable multi-agent orchestration under adversarial pressure, wrapped in a business that compounds.
144	
145	**The missing factor.** KINTSUGI v2 is linear and closed. Omega makes the system's value **compound with every failure it sees, across agents it has never seen, proven by people it does not control.** The shift is from *repair* to *immunity*.
146	
147	### 2.3 Requirements traceability

Produce a signed, independently checkable account of every infection, repair, prevention and economic decision.**
211

214	| Parameter | Default | Meaning |
215	|---|---|---|
216	| W | 24 h | The autonomy window |
217	| SLO_h | pass rate ≥ s_h (e.g. 0.90) and p95 latency ≤ l_h | Per-host reliability objective |

236	| Memory | Implicit (git history) | Explicit antibodies with provenance, versioned and quarantinable |

245	| Immunology | Omega concept | Implementation |
246	|---|---|---|
247	| Pathogen | A condition that causes failures | A fault in code, environment, model, prompt or data |
248	| Symptom | A failing or flagged trace | neatlogs span with an error, failed grader verdict, or detection hit |
249	| Innate pattern-recognition receptors | Baseline detections installed on every host | neatlogs Detections R‑001…R‑007 (§4.1.4) |

252	| Helper T cells (coordination) | Coordinator | Plans, budgets, settles disputes |
253	| B cells (antibody production) | Immunologist | Builds, matures and refines antibodies |
254	| Antibody | A verified, portable repair unit | `AB-*` (§5.8) |
255	| Adaptive receptor | A detection specific to one antibody | Created with `POST /detections` [V] |
256	| Affinity maturation | Cross-host maturation | The antibody must repair a *second* host before admission |
257	| Memory B cells | Antibody Library | Public git repo, every commit checkpointed by Entire |
258	| Secondary immune response | Recipe-first repair | Skips diagnosis; about 10× cheaper [I] |
259	| Vaccination | Motif scan, induced trigger, prophylactic patch | entire-graph snapshot + VF2 matching + Saboteur trigger |
260	| Immunological memory of past infections | Retroactive diagnosis | `POST /detections/{id}/backfills` [V] |
261	| Autoimmunity | A fix that harms a host | Canary SPRT → auto-revert → quarantine |
262	| Immune tolerance | Learned preconditions and negative motifs | `P_a` in the antibody |
263	| Metabolism and homeostasis | Budget governor | cfo.ai unit-economics model |
264	| Nervous system | Senses, memory, notary | neatlogs (afferent and efferent) and Entire (episodic memory, body map, notary) |

266	### 3.4 Formal model
267	
268	**Host.** h = ⟨R_h, w_h, E_h, SLO_h, v_h, λ_h, tier_h⟩, where:
269	- R_h is the repository;
270	- w_h is the neatlogs `workflow_name`;
271	- E_h = E_h^train ∪ E_h^hold is the evaluation suite, with the held-out split encrypted and hash-committed at T0;
272	- tier_h is the commercial tier in the cfo.ai model.
273	
274	**Failure signature.**
275	
276	```
277	φ(τ) = SHA-256( JCS( normalize(
278	    failing_span.kind, failing_span.name, tool_name,
279	    canonical_error_class,
280	    preceding_span_names[-3:],      # 3-gram of span names before the failure
281	    sorted(detection_ids_hit)
282	)))
283	```
284	
285	Normalisation removes IDs, numbers, timestamps, UUIDs and file paths below the repo root. It also maps library-specific errors to a canonical taxonomy, for example every HTTP 429 variant → `RateLimited`.
286	
287	**Incident.** ι = ⟨φ, h, {τ}, t_open, B_ι, state⟩, with state ∈ {OPEN, REPRODUCED, ATTRIBUTED, REPAIRING, SHIPPED, CANARY, RESOLVED, ESCALATED, PARKED}.
288	
289	**Antibody.** a = ⟨φ_a, receptor_a, M_a, P_a, recipe_a, contract_a, evidence_a, economics_a, lineage_a, state_a⟩, with state ∈ {CANDIDATE, MATURED, ACTIVE, QUARANTINED, RETIRED}.
290	
291	**Secondary-response match.** Antibody a applies to a new incident ι on host h when:
292	
293	```
294	(φ(ι) = φ_a  ∨  sim_semantic(ι, a) ≥ θ)  ∧  match(M_a, G_h) ≠ ∅  ∧  P_a(G_h) holds  ∧  state_a = ACTIVE
295	```
296	
297	**Invariants.** Every implementation MUST maintain these:
298	
299	- **I1.** No change made by Omega reaches a protected branch without passing G0–G7 (§5.11).
300	- **I2.** No commit lands on a protected branch inside W without a valid attestation (§4.5).
301	- **I3.** Every incident terminates in RESOLVED, ESCALATED or PARKED. Nothing is abandoned silently.
302	- **I4.** Cumulative spend per host per month stays within Pool_h (§4.6), which enforces the margin floor.
303	- **I5.** Held-out task content never enters any crew member's context except the Auditor's gate activity.
304	- **I6.** Sabotage specifications never enter crew context before the reveal. This is enforced with honeytokens (§7.2).
305	- **I7.** Every detection hit inside W maps to an incident or to a deduplication record. This is what proves there was no cherry-picking (§7.3).
306	
307	### 3.5 Compounding economics (Wright's law)
308	
309	#### 3.5.1 The law
310	
311	Wright's law says the unit cost of the n‑th repetition of a task falls as a power of cumulative volume:
312	
313	```
314	C_n = C_1 · n^(−b)
315	Progress ratio  PR = 2^(−b)       # cost multiplier for each doubling of cumulative repairs
316	Learning rate   LR = 1 − PR
317	```
318	
319	**Estimation.** Ordinary least squares on ln C_n = ln C_1 − b·ln n + ε, using actual costs per incident from neatlogs (§4.6.5). The standard error of b̂ comes from OLS, with a bootstrap confidence interval as a cross-check. b is fitted globally and per pathogen class. The fitted b̂ feeds the cfo.ai model as a cost driver.
320	
321	#### 3.5.2 Two mechanisms produce the curve
322	
323	1. **Secondary responses.** When an incident's pathogen class already has an ACTIVE antibody, Omega skips triage clustering, attribution and multi-hypothesis search. It runs recipe → gates → canary instead. Cost c_s ≪ c_p.
324	2. **Cheaper primary responses.** New incidents still get cheaper over time. Related antibodies act as hypothesis priors, the Archivist's graph cache warms up (`entire graph index`), and K (the number of forks) shrinks as priors get sharper.
325	
326	**Expected cost per incident:**
327	
328	```
329	E[C_ι](n) = q(n)·c_s + (1 − q(n))·c_p(n)
330	q(n) = probability that the incident's pathogen class is already covered by an ACTIVE antibody
331	```
332	
333	#### 3.5.3 Why q(n) rises fast: Zipf-distributed pathogens
334	
335	Agent failure classes are heavily skewed: a few classes (rate limits, state lost on retry, schema drift, loops, context overflow) dominate. Model the class frequencies as Zipf with exponent s over K classes:
336	
337	```
338	P(class k) ∝ k^(−s),   coverage after learning the m most frequent classes:
339	Q(m) = H_{m,s} / H_{K,s},   H_{m,s} = Σ_{k=1..m} k^(−s)
340	```
341	
342	Worked example [I], with K = 200 and s = 1.1:
343	
344	| Classes learned (m) | 5 | 10 | 20 | 50 | 100 |
345	|---|---|---|---|---|---|
346	| Incident coverage Q(m) | 45.8% | 57.0% | 67.9% | 81.5% | 91.0% |
347	
348	Because the most frequent classes are learned first, **learning only 20 classes covers about 68% of all incidents**.
349	
350	#### 3.5.4 Network effect
351	
352	With N hosts sharing one library, each pathogen class is learned once (primary cost c_p) and applied N times (secondary cost c_s). The per-host cost of a class therefore tends to c_p/N + c_s. Vaccination also lowers the incident rate itself:
353	
354	```
355	μ_eff = μ · (1 − v),   v = share of incidents prevented by vaccination
356	```
357	
358	#### 3.5.5 Worked unit economics [I]
359	
360	Assumptions: price P = $299 per host per month; monitoring cost C_mon = $18 per host per month; μ = 8 incidents per host per month; c_p = $14.00 (diagnosis $1.50, three Surgeons $6.00, gates and evals $5.00, canary $1.50); c_s = $1.60.
361	
362	| Fleet size N | q | E[C_ι] | Incident cost/host/month | COGS/host/month | Gross margin |
363	|---|---|---|---|---|---|
364	| 10 | 0.30 | $10.28 | $82.24 | $100.24 | **66.5%** |
365	| 100 | 0.70 | $5.32 | $42.56 | $60.56 | **79.7%** |
366	| 1,000 | 0.90 | $2.84 | $22.72 | $40.72 | **86.4%** |
367	
368	**Implied learning parameters.** Cumulative incidents per month grow 10× at each step (80 → 800 → 8,000). Cost falls by about 48% per decade, so b ≈ 0.28 and PR ≈ 0.82: **an 18% learning rate**, comparable to classic manufacturing learning curves [I].
369	
370	#### 3.5.6 Pricing implication
371	
372	Because marginal cost falls with scale, Omega can offer:
373	- a **per-host subscription**, whose margin grows with the network;
374	- an optional **outcome fee per prevented incident** (vaccination-confirmed), which aligns the price with value delivered.
375	
376	Both are modeled as scenarios in cfo.ai (§10).
377	
378	### 3.6 The compounding factor, stated precisely
379	
380	The curve is a **power law, not an exponential**. "Exponential" is marketing language; this spec says *compounding*.
381	
382	What compounds:
383	- **Cost per repair** falls with cumulative volume (Wright).
384	- **Coverage** rises steeply with the number of learned classes (Zipf).
385	- **Protection per antibody** grows linearly with fleet size (network effect).
386	
387	Together these make Omega's value per unit of spend **rise** as it sees more failures. That is the opposite of a linear repair service, and it is the property v2 was missing.
388	
389	---

392
